name: Yuliya Haranok
body:
There has been much written about the buyer journey shortening, but I think the more useful question is where along that journey a buyer meets you first, and whether your company has any say in the matter.

we all know that the majority of B2B buyers now form a meaningful view of a vendor before a sales conversation ever begins, and increasingly that view is shaped not by a single touchpoint but by a scattered, unpredictable set of them: a LinkedIn post read on a commute, a podcast clip surfaced by an algo, a summary an AI assistant generated on their behalf while researching a category they barely understood a week earlier.

We are not moving through a funnel in any tidy sense.

Better way to put is they/or we are assembling an impression from fragments, most of which the vendor never chose and often does not even know occurred.

This creates a worthy problem for companies who still plan content as a single asset published to a single channel. A blog post that lives only on your own site, however well researched, reaches a buyer who happens to search the exact right term at the exact right moment. Everyone else building the same impression through other channels, other formats, other algorithms, never encounters it at all.

I see 2 distinct failures in how companies typically respond to this.

(1) Treating distribution as an afterthought - something a junior marketer manually handles after the work of creation is finished, which in practice means it happens inconsistently/not at all once deadlines tighten.

(2) Treating every channel identically - posting the same asset everywhere in the same form, which mistakes presence for relevance. A buyer encountering a native, platform-appropriate version of your thinking trusts it considerably more than one who recognises a copy-pasted asset dropped somewhere it does not belong.

What works is treating a single piece of original thinking as raw material, and building platform-native versions of it deliberately, at a cadence that keeps the same idea circulating across the fragments a buyer is assembling their impression from.

You do not have to create more content. Reality is your buyer's journey through your brand happens on their terms, across surfaces you do not fully control, and your only genuine lever is making sure a well-considered version of your thinking is present wherever that assembly is happening.

Companies that treat distribution with the same rigour they apply to creation will without a doubt build a materially stronger presence in a buyer's mind.

name: Yuliya Haranok
body:
I’m a Founding Account Executive at Distribution.ai.

A software that turns one piece of content into dozens of marketing assets.

Founded by Ross Simmonds.

Today is Ross’ birthday, and I’ve been trying to figure out how to say what I want to say instead of the usual “happy birthday” post.

So let me try to share 3 stories with you.

1. The first one goes back to when he reached out to me about 6 months ago. I joined as a Founding AE, which also meant there was no playbook to follow. No perfect answers, no proven process, and no step-by-step guide telling me exactly what to do. Most of it has been figuring things out as we go.

I remember having chat where I wasn’t completely sure what the right answer was, or calls where I walked away thinking I could have handled something better. But one thing I’ve learned from him is to stay calm and trust the process. What I’ve learned building something from zero is that the instinct to wait until you’re fully confident before running a call is usually the wrong instinct.

You do things under-prepared, learn what worked and what didn’t, and then do it again. By 20 iterations you have an answer from you experience. That has probably been one of my biggest lessons from this experience so far.

2. The second story is about the person behind the name. Ross has built multiple businesses and is one of the most well-known names in this industry, so naturally, when you start working with someone like that, you have a certain expectation of what they’ll be like. But as I’ve gotten to know you, Ross, what has stood out to me most is how thoughtful you are. Whether we’re talking about work, solving a problem, or figuring out what comes next, you have a way of looking at things without making everything feel like a crisis. You’re genuinely one of the wisest people I’ve had the chance to know, and I think that’s something you notice even more once you get to work with you closely.

3. And last, but definitely not least - don’t be afraid to dance. Building companies, working hard, chasing goals and trying to make things happen is great, but you also have to enjoy the ride. Have fun when you’re with the people you love, be bold, don’t overthink everything, and don’t be afraid of being cringe. Sometimes you just have to put yourself out there, laugh at yourself, enjoy the moment and keep moving. Life is too short to constantly worry about whether you’re doing everything the “right” way.

So Ross, happy birthday. Thank you for trusting me, giving me the opportunity to build, and giving me the space to figure things out along the way.

Here’s to another year of building, learning, taking risks, and definitely a lot more dancing.

Happy birthday, Ross! 🎂

name: Yuliya Haranok
body:
Here is everything we've shipped in the last 30 days @ Distribution.io, because apparently I forget how much we’ve shipped until I stop and write it all down.

(1) Instagram reels & carousels - updated

You can now hand us a long video and we'll turn it into three short ones, subtitled, reframed, with descriptions and hashtags written for you. Last month, those clips only went to YouTube Shorts. Now they go to Instagram Reels too, which means one long video becomes a week's worth of Instagram posts without you touching the editing timeline. Carousels also take more images than before (up to 20 now). And we quietly strip URLs out of your Instagram posts, since Instagram won't make them clickable anyway. Small thing, but it's one less line item for you to catch when you're reviewing a post before it goes out.

(2) You can fix one line without rerolling the whole post

Last month we put an AI chat inside the product. This month we made it sharper, specifically, better at regenerating just a piece of your post. If there's one sentence that isn't landing, you highlight it, regenerate that part alone, and push straight to publishing. Before this, a weak opening line meant regenerating the entire post and gambling on losing copy you already liked. That trade-off is gone now. Everything outside your selection stays exactly as you left it.

(3) The link in your first comment

You can now send your link into the first comment automatically, write your own supporting text around it, and decide that behavior separately for each platform you post to. So the link stays in the post on X, but drops into the comment on LinkedIn: same underlying content, handled the way each platform actually rewards it.

(4) Custom instructions inside style preferences

Toggles get you close, but they were never going to cover every specific thing your brand does or refuses to do. So Style Preferences now takes written custom instructions, and you can attach files alongside them. Whatever you write there sits on top of your toggle choices when we generate content: it's where the rules that don't fit a setting finally live. Tell us how you handle product names. Ban the phrases you're sick of seeing. Upload a few posts that nailed it and let the generator learn from those directly.

(5) A queue built to save you time

Queue scheduling is more flexible now. You can edit time slot settings right inside the table, no more leaving the page to open a separate settings screen just to nudge when something fires. The calendar also remembers whatever view you left it in, so tomorrow, it's exactly where you left it today.

(6) The small stuff (which isn't really small0

Alongside the bigger releases, we kept working through a steady stream of smaller fixes: pages loading faster, buttons where you expect them, the edge cases that used to send you refreshing the page out of frustration. If you've flagged something to us and watched it quietly get fixed within the week, that's this process doing its job. So keep flagging things. It's working.

What's next?

Every feature above exists because someone was in the product, hit friction, and told us about it. If something in your workflow still feels slower or harder than it should, tell us that too. It’s one of the fastest ways to get an improvement onto the roadmap.

name: Yuliya Haranok
body:
For about 3 years, before any of the job titles on my profile, I co-founded a small volunteer group in Minsk called Prodobro.

We held over 70 events. Family-based orphanages, a neurological centre, kids who were mostly just trying to figure out how to talk to other kids, how to keep up at school, how to get through an afternoon.

I don't really know how to make that sound impressive on LinkedIn, and I'm not sure I want to.

There's no clean business lesson I'm going to pull out of it at the end of this post. I trained volunteers who sometimes didn't show up. I did PR nobody read. I chased small amounts of funding that took more effort than the amount justified.

I don't bring this up often. It doesn't fit neatly next to the rest of my work history, and I've never quite known how to talk about it without sounding like I'm reaching for a moral. Being honest, I don't think there is one.

I was going through some of the photos recently, and it brought me back to that time.

I was just showing up for people who had a harder week than I did, and some part of me has been quietly trying to live up to that since.

It made me realise how much that experience quietly stayed with me, and reminded me that sometimes our duty is simply to show up when we can. So I thought I'd share this, as a small reminder to myself, and maybe to someone else too.

Remember - You can't be too philosophical with people's hunger. Always pay it forward if you can.

Happy Sunday :)
